newsitem.title: UK: Dlr sets 39-mth high in Europe, then settles down.
newsitem.headline: Dlr sets 39-mth high in Europe, then settles down.

text.p: The dollar surged briefly to its highest level against the mark since February 1994, boosted by a yawning gap between unemployment rates in the U.S. and Germany and the prospect of a soft European single currency.
Labour market reports for May showed the unemployment rate in the U.S. fell to a 23-year low at 4.8 percent while the seasonally-adjusted German equivalent spiralled higher to 11.4.

The dollar's spike was short-lived, however, as traders grew wary of the speed of the mark's decline and the prospect of European central bank support to stabilise the situation. This prompted a wave of dollar profit-taking late in the session.

"The prospect of a U.S. rate hike in July has risen but the bottom line is that we've still got a picture of strong growth and benign inflation - this is the ideal combination for any currency," said Mark Geddes, treasury economist at ABN Amro.

Geddes said the dollar's upside is being capped, however, by periodic bouts of profit taking amid fears of official protest at the pace of its rise. Concerns about growing strength of the yen and stability of dollar/yen is also a drag, he said.
At 1450 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.7280/85 marks compared with 1.7292/97 late Thursday and down from a fresh 1997 peak at 1.7423 set shortly after the U.S. jobs report.

U.S. non-farm payrolls rose a lower than expected 138,000 in May but the April rise was revised sharply higher to 323,000 from 142,000. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.8 percent from 4.9 percent and average hourly earnings climbed 0.3 percent.
The report is seen as possibly increasing the chance of a quarter-point rise in the Federal Funds rate to 5.75 percent when the Fed's policy-making Open Market Committee meets on July 1 and 2.

This stands in stark contrast to the German jobs report released earlier in the day, which showed a seasonally-adjusted rise of 56,000 in German unemployed and a rise in the unemployment rate to 11.4 percent from 11.2 percent in April.

Analysts said the continued weakness of the German labour market was damaging to the mark from two angles. First, it reinforces the low interest rate environment in Germany and secondly, it make it more difficult for Germany to meet its budget deficit goals in time for European monetary union.
The latter has stoked expectations this week Germany will, as a result, be forced to accept a broad-based start to EMU with a looser interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty criteria.
"The market will be more prepared to question the wilingness of the central bankers to keep the dollar capped then before," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan.

"A strong dollar is one supportive force for the German economy and the government's attempt to better its fiscal position," said Persaud. "Recent events have reinforced our dollar/mark bull forecast."

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer and senior council members Johann-Wilhelm Gaddum and Reimut Jochimsen all moved today to downplay speculation that the post-EMU budget stability pact would be watered down.
The new Socialist government in France, in power since Monday, has made repeated noises during the week about the need to renegotiate the stability pact.

Dealers said there was some concern about taking aggressive positions, however, as the outside risk that EMU is delayed could still spark a knee-jerk move back into marks. European Union finance ministers meet in Luxembourg on Sunday and Monday.

Sterling shrugged off a quarter-point rise in key UK interest rates, meantime. The move was made after the first meeting of the Bank of England's newly formed monetary policy committee and was expected by many in the market.
Analysts said rates would now be on hold and their future trajectory would depend on the details of the July 2 budget.
